authored_explainer.title: Cereal Production Is 1.5x Higher Than In 1972
authored_explainer.hook: The 1970s predicted food shortages; the data shows a very different harvest.
says: Progression to secondary school rose from 77.8% in 1985 to 91.3% in 2017—1.2 times higher, opening education to more students.
Cereal production climbed from 1083.7 million metric tons in 1972 to 1644.1 million in 2024—1.5 times higher, feeding a much larger world.
China leads farmland at 5.2 million square kilometers; the United States 4.2, Australia 3.6, Brazil 2.4, Russia 2.2—an enormous food-production base.
authored_explainer.closing: The feared famine missed how education, grain output, and farmland could sustain more people.
authored_explainer.question: Which changed most: school, grain, or land?

authored_explainer.title: Waste Energy Is 3.0x Higher Than In 1990
authored_explainer.hook: Since 1990, one energy source tripled—and it wasn't solar or wind.
says: In 1990, combustible renewables and waste supplied 10.2% of energy; by 2024, 30.1%—3.0 times higher, turning discards into fuel.
Electricity access rose from 73.2% in 1998 to 91.9% in 2024—1.3 times higher, bringing power to far more people.
Waste methane emissions grew from 903.8 Mt CO2e in 1972 to 1,652 Mt CO2e in 2024—1.8 times higher, raising the climate bill.
authored_explainer.closing: Waste now powers more lives, but its methane cost means disposal choices still matter.
authored_explainer.question: Which changed most: fuel, power, or waste?

authored_explainer.title: Population Growth Fell 54% Since 1972
authored_explainer.hook: Population kept rising, but its growth rate nearly stopped accelerating.
says: Rural population fell from 63.1% in 1972 to 42.2% in 2025—67 percent of its old share, shifting daily life toward cities.
The largest city's share moved from 18.2% in 1972 to 16.2% in 2025—barely changed, even as urbanization spread beyond one hub.
Population growth dropped from 2 annual % in 1972 to 0.91 annual % in 2025—46 percent of its old pace, slowing expansion.
authored_explainer.closing: A slower growth rate reshapes schools, housing, and work long before population shrinks.
authored_explainer.question: Which shift matters most: rural, city, or growth?
